- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., > -0.22 over recent days), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope to avoid overbought bias.
- If sentiment is positive and price is trending upward, model often overestimates future gains; cap forecast growth at 10–15% above recent 7-day average to avoid overfitting.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed, model tends to lag behind true price; add 1–2 days of lagged price momentum to forecast to capture delayed reaction.
- Mean reversion is strong in low-volatility periods; if sentiment is weak and price is near 30-day moving average, reduce forecast by 2–5% to reflect reversion bias.
- In multi-day forecast horizons (e.g., 30d), model often fails to capture sentiment-driven volatility; weight sentiment more heavily in early days (e.g., 1–3 days) to adjust for sentiment momentum.
